ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A hemispherical hollow shell with an inner radius of $R$ and an outer radius of $R^{\prime}{=}\sqrt{2}R$ is made of glass with a refractive index of $n=\sqrt{2}$. A beam of light parallel to the central symmetry axis $O O^{\prime}$ is incident on the outer surface of this hemisphere. To ensure that no light exits from the inner surface of the shell, a circular light-blocking plate with its center passing through the $O O^{\prime}$ axis must be placed above the shell, perpendicular to $O O^{\prime}$.

1. What is the radius $d$ of the light shield?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A hemispherical hollow shell with an inner radius of $R$ and an outer radius of $R' = \sqrt{2}R$ is made of glass with refractive index $n = \sqrt{2}$. A beam of light parallel to the central symmetry axis $OO'$ is incident on the outer surface of the hemisphere. To ensure that no light exits from the inner surface of the shell, a circular light-blocking plate whose center lies on the $OO'$ axis must be placed above the shell, perpendicular to $OO'$. What is the radius $d$ of the light shield?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure draws a cross-section of a hemispherical hollow shell with O as the common center of the circle; the inner and outer boundaries are concentric semicircles; the vertical dashed line is the central axis of symmetry OO', and multiple light rays go downward from above and are parallel to one another, indicating that the incident light is parallel to OO'. The radius R is marked on the inner semicircle; the light-blocking plate is not drawn in the figure, but the problem statement requires the light-blocking plate to be a circular plate with OO' as its axis. Reasoning: Take a vertical incident light ray whose horizontal distance from the axis OO' is b. When it strikes the outer surface with outer radius R' = √2 R, the normal to the outer surface is the radius passing through the incident point, so the angle of incidence i satisfies sin i = b/R'. Light enters glass with refractive index n = √2 from air; by Snell's law, sin r = sin i / n = b/(nR'), where r is the angle of refraction of the refracted ray relative to the inward radial direction. The refracted ray propagates in a straight line in the glass. The perpendicular distance from this straight line to the center O is h = R' sin r = R' · b/(nR') = b/n. When this ray reaches the inner surface with inner radius R, the angle of incidence j satisfies sin j = h/R = b/(nR). The critical angle j_c from glass to air satisfies sin j_c = 1/n. If sin j < 1/n, that is, b/(nR) < 1/n, then b < R, and this kind of ray will emerge from the inner surface; if b ≥ R, then it reaches or exceeds the critical condition and will not emerge outward from the inner surface. Therefore, to ensure that no light emerges from the inner surface, the light-blocking plate must block all incident rays with b < R. The light-blocking plate has OO' as its central axis, so its radius should be taken as d = R.
